Chapter 3: Staying Present with Pain and Difficulty
You know, it’s completely normal to want to escape pain. Most of us look for distractions—maybe we keep ourselves busy, binge-watch TV, or scroll endlessly on our phones—just hoping to find a little relief from what hurts. But here’s the thing: the more we try to outrun pain, the more it seems to catch up with us. It lingers in the background, growing stronger the more we avoid it.
Let me tell you about a man in his forties who lost his job. He started filling his days with television and social media, trying to drown out that heavy emptiness. For a while, it worked. But the relief never lasted. The pain kept coming back, sharper than ever. One night, instead of reaching for another distraction, he just sat quietly. No screens, no noise. At first, the sadness and fear felt almost too much to handle. But as he kept breathing and allowed those feelings to be there, something shifted. The pain didn’t vanish, but it became less overwhelming, even a little less scary.
Choosing to stay present with pain—it’s a bold move. It goes against every instinct to run away. But honestly, it’s the only way we can really understand and transform our suffering. That’s where mindfulness comes in. It’s all about paying attention—right here, right now—without judging what we find. Mindfulness lets us notice our patterns of avoidance, the sneaky ways our mind tries to escape, and gently brings us back to the present moment.
Think about a young woman grieving after a breakup. She kept replaying old memories, imagining different endings, wishing she could make the pain disappear. Instead of pushing the hurt away, she tried something different. She just sat and noticed the ache in her chest, let the tears come and go. And in that space, she found a bit of tenderness beneath the pain—a quiet reminder of how deeply she’d loved.
Staying present with tough emotions doesn’t mean getting stuck or wallowing in them. It’s about letting feelings come and go, like waves rolling onto the shore. Over time, this simple practice actually builds resilience. Your heart learns it can survive pain; it doesn’t have to be broken by it.
Here’s something a lot of people don’t realize: when you meet pain with awareness, it can actually teach you something. It shines a light on your most vulnerable places, the habits that keep repeating, the needs that haven’t been met. In this way, suffering turns into a kind of guide, pointing you toward healing.
Now, I won’t pretend it’s easy. This practice takes patience, gentleness, and a real willingness to sit with what’s uncomfortable. But as you learn to stay present with your pain, you discover a whole new strength—a strength that comes from facing difficulty with an open heart, not from turning away.
